findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin controller, route, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records. Operators cannot populate the table outside of hand-running console inserts, so BlockedEmail.should_block? always queries an empty table and the entire email-blocking feature is inert in any real deployment until someone hand-crafts rows.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a synchronous SELECT plus UPDATE (record.save) inside the User email validation, a side-effecting DB write on a path that previously did no database work during validation. Every signup (and any user save with email_changed?) pays an extra query plus write; concurrent signup attempts matching the same blocked address serialize on that single row's UPDATE lock, which a spam flood hitting a blocked address turns into row-lock contention during account creation.

[BUG] The client adds result.values.email to rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present, but server-side errors.email is populated for any email validation failure — including 'has already been taken' from the uniqueness validation — not only blocked-email rejections. A failed signup due to a duplicate email pushes that address into rejectedEmails, after which the emailValid computed property (which now observes rejectedEmails.@each) permanently reports the generic 'invalid' failure for that address in the open modal, even though the actual problem was that the email is taken, not that it is disallowed.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact, case-sensitive lookup (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)), so a blocked address is only matched when the signup submits the identical casing, unlike the sibling domain blacklist in the same validator which matches case-insensitively via Regexp.new(..., true). A user blocked as 'bad@spamclub.com' signs up as 'BAD@spamclub.com' or 'Bad@spamclub.com' and the validator passes them through (and, because the unique index on email is case-sensitive, two rows for the same address can coexist); the PR's core acceptance criterion — blocking a given email — is evaded by a case change, and additionally by plus-addressing ('user+tag@gmail.com') since no normalization precedes the lookup.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table, model, and validator ship with no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, controller action, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records (the only producer is the spec fabricator). Operators cannot actually use the feature after deploy: the table stays empty and should_block? always returns false, so 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' is inert until someone writes rows via the Rails console; the do_nothing action_type is likewise unreachable, having no setting path at all.

[ADVISORY] The new failure-payload contract (errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: user.attributes.slice(...)) has no verification anywhere in this diff: the added specs cover only EmailValidator and BlockedEmail, and no spec asserts users_controller#create emits these keys. The client hard-depends on this exact shape (create_account_controller.js pushes result.values.email only when result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values); a regression that renames or drops either key silently disables the client-side rejectedEmails cache with no failing test, degrading the feature back to flash-message-only with nothing catching it.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely and exercises only the blocked-email branch, leaving the whitelist/blacklist domain-restriction logic moved into this diff (validator lines 5-12) with zero assertions. A regression in the relocated domain restriction code — e.g. the gsub('.', '\.') escaping or the whitelist-vs-blacklist elsif ordering — ships green because the only test file for the class never reaches those branches; this is also a coverage regression relative to intent, since the logic moved classes and its old call site (User#email_validator) was deleted in the same diff.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write (load record, match_count += 1, record.save) inside User validation, so concurrent signup attempts against the same blocked address lose increments, and any surrounding transaction rollback on the user-creation path discards the write entirely. match_count and last_match_at — the statistics the schema comment says admins will use to see whether emails were ever hit — undercount under concurrency and are silently erased when the enclosing user-create transaction (statement-invalid rescue or later failure) rolls back; a validation hook that writes is also executed on every User save with a changed email, including admin edits, inflating the counters.

[ADVISORY] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails for any entry under result.errors.email, which includes uniqueness and whitelist/blacklist failures, and the rejectedEmails list is never cleared or scoped by error type. A user whose signup failed because the email was already taken gets that address permanently rendered as generic 'invalid' in emailValidated for the rest of the session (the message key shown is user.email.invalid, not the taken-email reason), so the form contradicts the flash message that correctly says the email is taken; there is also no spec for the create_account_controller change covering this path.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table is created but the diff contains no writer anywhere — no admin controller, route, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path populates BlockedEmail records, so the blocklist cannot be populated by any operator action. The feature ships inert: site admins have no way to add a blocked email, so should_block? always finds no record and the entire blocking path is dead code until someone hand-inserts rows into the database. This is under-scoping of the stated intent (blocking emails) to only the enforcement half.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? matches with `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)`, an exact case-sensitive equality lookup, so any case variation of a blocked address bypasses the block. An admin blocks 'spam@evil.com'; a registrant signs up with 'SPAM@evil.com' or 'Spam@evil.com' and passes validation (PostgreSQL string comparison is case-sensitive by default), defeating the feature's stated purpose for the cheapest possible evasion. Same for the unique index on email, which stores variants as distinct rows.

[BUG] The client pushes the email into rejectedEmails on ANY email error in the response (result.errors.email is populated for uniqueness 'has already been taken' and whitelist/blacklist 'not_allowed' failures, not just blocked-email failures), permanently marking that email invalid for the browser session. A user whose email is merely already taken gets the field pinned to the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' message via the emailValidated check at lines 68-74, overriding any subsequent server state; even if the blocking account is deleted or the admin unblocks the address, the client keeps rejecting it until a full page reload, because rejectedEmails is never cleared or revalidated against the server.

[ADVISORY] should_block? writes match_count and last_match_at statistics on every matching validation (including for action_type :do_nothing records), but nothing in the diff reads these columns. Every signup attempt matching a record takes a read-modify-write UPDATE on the signup hot path to maintain telemetry with no consumer — no admin screen, report, or query in this diff surfaces match_count/last_match_at — so the write cost is paid for data nobody can see; it is also a non-atomic counter increment that loses matches under concurrent signups.

[ADVISORY] The new response contract (errors: user.errors.to_hash, values: name/username/email) that the JavaScript client depends on has no test anywhere in this diff. The create_account_controller's rejectedEmails mechanism silently breaks (no email ever gets pushed, or a shape change raises) if the payload keys or the slice'd attribute names change; a regression here fails with no signal because no spec pins the errors/values structure the client parses.

[ADVISORY] The spec for the new EmailValidator only exercises the BlockedEmail branch (with should_block? stubbed) and never tests the domain whitelist/blacklist logic that was moved into this class from User#email_validator. The relocated email_in_restriction_setting? code — including its regex construction with gsub('.', '\.') — has no coverage in its new home; a regression in the moved domain-restriction logic (e.g. the regex escaping) would pass the suite while silently disabling or inverting domain restrictions for all signups.

[BUG] should_block? increments match_count via a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then record.save), so two concurrent registrations matching the same blocked email both read N and write N+1, losing one increment. match_count silently undercounts under concurrency, and last_match_at can be overwritten with an older timestamp; the statistics this table exists to collect drift from reality with no error raised. The increment must be an atomic UPDATE (update_all("match_count = match_count + 1", ...) or increment_counter).

[BUG] validate_each mutates persistent state: BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) performs a SELECT plus an UPDATE (match_count/last_match_at) inside a validation, making User#valid? a state-changing operation. Any code path that validates a User without saving (a valid? probe, a save that later fails on another attribute or a DB error, admin/email-change flows re-validating) still increments match_count and bumps last_match_at, so the counters track validation executions rather than actual blocked registration attempts; the data the admin is meant to read (has this address ever been blocked?) is inflated by noise, and every such validation pays a SELECT+UPDATE on the user-creation hot path.

[BUG] The block lookup BlockedEmail.where(email: email) uses case-sensitive equality while the domain blacklist check in the same validator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb line 21, Regexp.new(..., true)) is explicitly case-insensitive, so the two mechanisms in one file disagree on email canonical form. A blocked entry stored as 'Spammer@X.com' (or a submission whose case differs from the stored entry) does not match, so the exact-address block is bypassed by a case variation — the very trick the adjacent case-insensitive domain rule defends against — and the case-sensitive unique index additionally permits duplicate rows differing only in case.

[BUG] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails on ANY result.errors.email, conflating 'blocked/not allowed' with 'email has already been taken' (the uniqueness validation also reports under :email), then renders the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for all of them. A legitimate user whose email already exists on the site gets that email silently poisoned in rejectedEmails: on the next attempt the controller short-circuits at the rejectedEmails check (lines 68-74) and shows 'must be a valid email address' for a perfectly valid email, with no server round-trip and no way to clear the state except reloading — the sentinel meaning of errors.email ('some email validation failed') is treated by the client as 'this email is invalid'.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table ships with no writer path anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, controller action, API route, rake task, or seed populates it; the only writes are the automatic match_count/last_match_at bumps in should_block?. Operators cannot actually block any email address: the model, migration, validator integration, and specs all exist, but unless the admin surface lands in a separate change the feature is inert — EmailValidator's BlockedEmail check queries an always-empty table on every user creation for zero effect.

[ADVISORY] action_type is an unconstrained integer column with no CHECK (or enum type at the DB level); only the Rails Enum maps 0/1 to :block/:do_nothing, and the lookup 'record.action_type == actions[:block]' fails open for any other value. Any row inserted outside ActiveRecord (raw SQL, a future bulk-import script) with an unmapped action_type is silently treated as do_nothing — the block is skipped with no error — where a CHECK constraint (action_type IN (0,1)) would fail loudly at write time.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails feature ships with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, controller action, API endpoint, rake task, or seed path creates BlockedEmail records, so the table and the EmailValidator branch wired to it are inert. Operators cannot actually block any email address after deploying this change; the accepted objective ('block emails') silently shrank to unreachable plumbing, and the match_count/last_match_at statistics built into should_block? imply a curation workflow that does not exist. Only someone with Rails console access can populate the table, which is not an operational path.

[ADVISORY] should_block? matches the submitted email by exact verbatim string ('BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first') with no case folding or plus-address normalization, so the block is trivially evadable. An attacker blocked as 'spam@spamclub.com' signs up as 'SPAM@spamclub.com' or 'spam+1@spamclub.com' and the block never fires; the feature's core purpose (preventing a specific address from re-registering) fails under the first trivial variation, and each miss still counts as a clean signup.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a non-atomic read-modify-write ('record.match_count += 1; record.save') and ignores the save's return value, so concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose counter increments and any failed save is silently swallowed. Under concurrent registration attempts the match_count statistic drifts low (lost updates, no atomic UPDATE), and if the save fails (e.g., a concurrent duplicate insert racing the unique index) the method still returns the action_type verdict with no log or signal — statistics silently under-report with no error surfaced.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails branch reuses I18n.t('user.email.invalid') for policy-blocked emails while the diff's new locale key 'user.email.blocked' ("is not allowed.") is added server-side only and never reaches the signup form's inline validation. A user whose email is admin-blocked is told their email is 'invalid' — implying a typo/format problem they will repeatedly try to 'fix' — instead of being told the address is not allowed; the message this PR introduces into server.en.yml is dead text as far as the primary signup UI is concerned.

[ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails guard is a raw string-equality check ('this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)') against result.values.email echoed back by the server, so any server-side normalization of the email (e.g., downcasing before validation) makes the guard a silent no-op. If the server normalizes case, result.values.email is stored lowercase while accountEmail retains the user's typed casing, contains() never matches, and the entire client-side 'remember rejected emails' behavior added in this diff does nothing — the user gets no inline invalidation and only the flash message from the previous failure.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec stubs out should_block? entirely and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist branch (email_in_restriction_setting? and the 'not_allowed' error) that was just moved out of User into this class. The relocated domain-restriction logic — half of the new validator's behavior, including its regex construction ('setting.gsub('.', '\.')') — has no test at its new home in this diff; a regression introduced during the move (e.g., the escaped-dot handling or the elsif ordering) ships uncaught, and future edits to the validator have no safety net for that branch.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs an exact, case-sensitive lookup (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no canonicalization, so the admin-managed blocklist is defeated by any case variation of the blocked address. An admin blocks 'bad@spammers.org'; an attacker registers with 'Bad@spammers.org' or 'BAD@SPAMMERS.ORG' and the lookup finds no row, so should_block? returns false and signup succeeds — the block feature does not block. The domain blacklist/whitelist check in the same validator uses Regexp.new(..., true) (case-insensitive), so the two controls normalize differently and the stricter control is the one that is case-sensitive.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? anchors the domain regex only at '@' and matches a substring, so a whitelist entry 'example.com' is satisfied by 'attacker@example.com.evil.org'. When SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist is in use (the restrictive direction of the control), an attacker registers with attacker@example.com.anything.tld and passes the whitelist restriction intended to limit signups to a specific domain; the diff carries this logic forward verbatim from the deleted user.rb email_validator, so the rewrite opportunity was missed.

[ADVISORY] The admin-set SiteSetting value is interpolated unescaped into Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") — only '.' is escaped, so any other regex metacharacter in the setting alters the pattern, and a crafted setting can produce catastrophic backtracking executed on every signup validation. A config value like 'a+|b' or '(/.*)*x' is treated as regex syntax rather than literal domain text, producing an over- or under-matching blacklist or a ReDoS stall on the account-creation path; per the config-backed-sink threat model the setting should be treated as attacker-influenceable input, not a trusted literal.

[ADVISORY] Blocked emails return the distinct i18n message 'user.email.blocked' ('is not allowed.') while domain-blacklist rejections return 'user.email.not_allowed', giving unauthenticated signup probes a distinguishable response that confirms a specific address is on the admin blocklist. An attacker scripts the signup endpoint and, by comparing the returned error text (and the per-request match_count increment observable as a state change), enumerates the exact contents of the site's blocklist — information intended to be admin-visible only.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never configures SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist, so both domain-restriction branches in lib/validators/email_validator.rb (lines 8-15) — the logic migrated out of user.rb's email_validator — are never exercised by any test in this diff. A regression in email_in_restriction_setting? (e.g., the escaping of '.' or the case-insensitive Regexp.new(..., true) flag) passes this spec silently; coverage of that migrated logic depends entirely on pre-existing user_spec tests that this diff does not touch or update, so the spec titled 'EmailValidator' actually verifies only the new blocked-email branch.

[ADVISORY] The 'adds an error when email matches a blocked email' test asserts only record.errors[:email].should be_present and never asserts which message was added, so it cannot distinguish the user.email.blocked error from a user.email.not_allowed error. A regression in validate_each that adds the wrong I18n key (not_allowed instead of blocked, e.g. if the restriction branch erroneously fires first) or that adds the error under a different attribute passes this spec, and users of a blocked email would see the wrong rejection message with no test failure.

[BUG] The diff adds the blocked_emails migration and the BlockedEmail model/validator but does not update db/schema.rb, so the review-base schema and the migration's schema drift apart: any environment that builds its schema from schema.rb (fresh installs, CI setups that skip migrations) has no blocked_emails table while the new code queries it unconditionally. On a schema.rb-provisioned database, every user signup runs EmailValidator#validate_each, which calls BlockedEmail.should_block? and executes BlockedEmail.where(email: ...) against a nonexistent table, raising ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid; user creation fails (the rescue in UsersController#create converts it to a generic error) rather than the schema matching what the code reads.

[ADVISORY] should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (read record, match_count += 1, record.save) with the save result ignored, so concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email lose increments and a failing save is swallowed with no log or error. Two concurrent signups with the same blocked address both read match_count=N and both write N+1, silently losing an increment; if record.save returns false (validation/connection failure) nothing is surfaced — the admin's match statistics silently undercount with no observable error anywhere.

[BUG] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails for ANY email validation error (uniqueness 'already taken', whitelist/blacklist 'not_allowed'), not just blocked-email rejections, and emailValid then reports the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' for that address regardless of the real server-side cause. A user who typo'd an already-registered email gets that address permanently marked rejected for the session; on retry the email field shows 'invalid' (submitDisabled keeps the form locked) instead of the actual 'already taken' reason, misdirecting the user and anyone debugging the report.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs its match_count/last_match_at DB write inside validate_each, outside the user-save transaction, so the increment persists even when the user record is never saved (e.g., password or username validation fails afterwards), and any path that validates the record twice increments twice. BlockedEmail match statistics count signup attempts that were ultimately rejected for unrelated reasons (or counted multiple times per attempt), so match_count no longer means 'successful blocked signup attempts' and admin decisions based on it are inflated.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail lookup and the unique index are case-sensitive exact matches, so a blocked entry 'Spammer@x.com' neither matches a signup with 'spammer@x.com' nor prevents a second record with different casing from being created. On PostgreSQL (case-sensitive collation) a blocked address is bypassed by simply changing the case of the local part, and the unique index permits duplicate block entries differing only in case, silently weakening the block the feature exists to enforce.

[ADVISORY] The diff ships the blocked_emails table and model with no writer anywhere — no admin UI, controller, rake task, or seed path populates the table, so the blocking behavior is inert until someone inserts rows manually via the console. An operator deploying this change gets no way to actually block an email address (the email_domains_blacklist path is the only working one); the new validation, client-side rejection tracking, and migration are all dead weight until raw console inserts are performed.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

Within this diff, there is no non-test code path that creates or manages `BlockedEmail` records (only specs/fabricator create them), so the new blocking capability is effectively unused unless records are created out-of-band. However, from the diff alone we cannot prove there isn't already an admin/API path elsewhere in the repo, so it's best treated as an integration/completeness concern rather than a definite functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (read record, match_count += 1, record.save) with the save result ignored, so concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email lose increments and a failing save is swallowed with no log or error. Two concurrent signups with the same blocked address both read match_count=N and both write N+1, silently losing an increment; if record.save returns false (validation/connection failure) nothing is surfaced — the admin's match statistics silently undercount with no observable error anywhere.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save` without any locking/atomic update and without checking the `save` return value. This is a classic read-modify-write race: concurrent calls can both read the same `match_count` and both write back `N+1`, losing an increment. Also, if `record.save` returns `false` (or fails silently in some cases), nothing is logged/handled, so match stats can be silently wrong.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails for ANY email validation error (uniqueness 'already taken', whitelist/blacklist 'not_allowed'), not just blocked-email rejections, and emailValid then reports the generic I18n 'user.email.invalid' for that address regardless of the real server-side cause. A user who typo'd an already-registered email gets that address permanently marked rejected for the session; on retry the email field shows 'invalid' (submitDisabled keeps the form locked) instead of the actual 'already taken' reason, misdirecting the user and anyone debugging the report.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on any failed create where `result.errors.email` is present, the code pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` (no check for the specific error type/message): `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email); }`. Then `emailValid` short-circuits for any email in `rejectedEmails` and returns `failed: true` with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of whether the server-side error was uniqueness, whitelist/blacklist (`user.email.not_allowed`), blocked (`user.email.blocked`), etc. Because the computed property depends on `rejectedEmails.@each`, that generic failure will persist for that email for the rest of the session (even if the user re-enters the same address), misreporting the cause and potentially disabling submission if the UI gates on `emailValid`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs its match_count/last_match_at DB write inside validate_each, outside the user-save transaction, so the increment persists even when the user record is never saved (e.g., password or username validation fails afterwards), and any path that validates the record twice increments twice. BlockedEmail match statistics count signup attempts that were ultimately rejected for unrelated reasons (or counted multiple times per attempt), so match_count no longer means 'successful blocked signup attempts' and admin decisions based on it are inflated.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, `validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when there are no prior email errors, and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB update (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `save`) every time a matching record exists. Because this side effect happens during validation (not tied to a successful `User` save) and Rails can run validations multiple times, the stats can be incremented even if the `User` is never persisted or gets validated twice. However, the diff/specs do not define `match_count` as “successful blocked signups only”; it may be intended to count match/attempts, so this is more a semantics/architecture concern than a clearly incorrect behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail lookup and the unique index are case-sensitive exact matches, so a blocked entry 'Spammer@x.com' neither matches a signup with 'spammer@x.com' nor prevents a second record with different casing from being created. On PostgreSQL (case-sensitive collation) a blocked address is bypassed by simply changing the case of the local part, and the unique index permits duplicate block entries differing only in case, silently weakening the block the feature exists to enforce.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, and the model/index use plain `email` (`validates :email, ... uniqueness: true` and `add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`) with no downcasing/CI collation. On PostgreSQL this makes both the match and uniqueness constraint case-sensitive, so `Spammer@x.com` won’t match `spammer@x.com` and duplicate blocked entries differing only by case can be created, weakening the blocking behavior the diff introduces.
